This was probably a hard book to adapt, but their approach doesn't do it any favors. Some scenes are very literally translated to screen, with tons of exposition and explanation between them removed. I feel like we get the worst of both worlds here. Lots of wandering around aimlessly in the woods and bickering, without the benefit of a compelling mystery (which even the book didn't convincingly sell). Perhaps the worst part is the acting. Almost everyone looks bored at this point, and they're given only the most banal dialogue to keep the plot moving. You'd hardly believe these kids are supposed to be best friends of six years. The depiction of magic here is also quite uninspiring; wands are basically just guns.

Siento que esta película simplemente no funciona conmigo. Entiendo lo que intenta hacer y por qué tiene un tono mucho más serio, pero se me hace demasiado pesada y bastante menos entretenida que las anteriores. La idea de tener a Harry, Ron y Hermione prácticamente solos durante gran parte de la película podría haberme encantado, pero el ritmo hace que algunos momentos se me hagan eternos. Hay escenas que visualmente son preciosas y otras que me parecen muy buenas, pero me cuesta sentir esa emoción que tenía con las primeras entregas. También creo que aquí se nota muchísimo el cambio de tono de la saga. Todo es gris, triste y oscuro, y personalmente echo muchísimo de menos la magia, el humor y la sensación de estar descubriendo el mundo de Hogwarts que tenían las primeras. No me parece una película horrible, porque tiene momentos muy potentes y la historia sigue siendo interesante, pero como experiencia me resulta bastante fría y aburrida en comparación con las demás.

Nick Cave's "O Children" is doing career-best work here, and I resent it deeply for being wasted on this scene. Two people slow dance in a tent for absolutely no narrative reason beyond "the other one left the room," and somehow the movie wants me to feel something warm about it. I do not. I feel the specific discomfort of watching Ron's worst suspicions about his own crush confirmed in real time, and he's not even there to object. The Ron-less stretch should just have been Hermione crying, Harry carefully avoiding the word "Ron" like it's a landmine, and a silence Harry doesn't know how to fill, because he doesn't know how to deal with emotional women. That's the scene. That's the whole scene. But naturally the script's solution is "put on music, problem solved." It feels like two actors got a note that said: "dance like you're together, so people will question if this should have been a thing." Beautiful needle drop, genuinely upsetting choreography of feelings, zero actual conversation to back any of it up. I'd rather rewatch the tent scenes where nothing happens than this one where something almost happens and shouldn't have.

(2.6) "I can't carry it for you, but I can give up and run away and then come back later." Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows: Part 1 has the same problems as the last installment but one: there are scenes with more than one color. The abhorrent imitation of Hong Kong cinema is finally set aside, the monochromatic filters are gone, and you can pause the film and see more than one color at a time. It's so refreshing to see the characters stand out against the backgrounds, to see environments with personality again. Grimmauld Place doesn't feel the same as the Ministry of Magic; each forest has a slightly different feel to it as the scene demands. It's such a breath of fresh air, and adds so much life to this installment. Unfortunately, the main gripe I had with the last film persists. Scenes are simplified, stripped of what made them important, and are completely ruined, from a cinematic standpoint. Take Umbridge's reveal: the book built up that she had returned with Mundungus unable to name her, describing her vaguely before saying she looked like a toad and Harry's scar tingling as he (and the reader) realizes who the trio are up against. But they show her early in the film during the anti-Harry propoganda montage, even giving her a close-up laugh just to make sure you didn't miss her, long before we see Mundungus captured. Similarly, they reveal that Bagshot is Nagini a beat too early, showing her speaking Parseltongue instead of English. I suppose that was for the audience's benefit, to realize something was wrong before the snake lunge? But anybody who is familiar enough with the franchise to remember what Parseltongue sounds like has probably read the books, and knows the twist, so why try to make it a twist? And why reveal the information early? As usual, several scenes are cut down or omitted outright. Wormtail's mercy, and subsequent murder? Cut. Why? I don't know, maybe for the rating. Kreacher's humanity, and love for Regulus, and subsequent respect for Harry? Trimmed down to the barest bones, offering none of the substantative weight behind the character. Harry disarming Draco, a major point that fuels the whole twist behind who masters the Elder Wand in the finale? Cut, now Harry just wrestles the wand from Draco's grip. And every scene just stops on a dime once the danger is over. The Rook explodes as the trio apparate away, and then we're in a calm establishing shot of a big field. Hermione banishes Nagini out the window of the Potter's house and then we smash cut to the duo sitting in the woods again. It's only really a problem in the second half of the film; dangers and escapes are strung together pretty well in the first half, but it's so distracting when the film gives up and decides it doesn't need the connective tissue. We've just got to see archival footage of various characters with big red x's on them to demonstrate they've died. It's an incredibly necessary scene. Showcase the book's thematic web about loyalty? Draw parralels between Harry's wavering loyalty to Dumbledore, Ron's loyalty to the quest, Xeno's loyalty wavering in the face of Luna's capture, Wormtail's loyalty leading to his demise, Dobby's loyalty getting him killed, or Kreacher's loyalty to Regulus? Nah, that's not particularly important. As long as we've copied the scene out of the book, we'll be good. A handful of nitpicks, before I wrap this up. Why does the Rook have a television in it, on the lower floor? Why does Voldemort, a character infatuated by magic who loves lording his prowess, choke Ollivander physically, with his hand? Why does the new all-magical Ministry still use Muggle toilets as entrances? Why is there even more Harmonie coding when that's not the endgame? Why does Dobby wear his shoddy pillowcase, when he's a free elf? Methinks they didn't want to spend the money to update the model. Why have a scene where Death Eaters stop the Hogwarts Express? By including that scene, you're suggesting that Voldemort held a big important meeting and assigned troops to infiltrate the train. Was one specifically assigned to stand on the tracks and hold up his hand, or was that guy just improvising? Why does Voldemort literally mock Lucius like a grade-schooler when taking his wand? It's not intimidating, or a demonstration of vanity. It's just silly. People love to argue that the series gets darker as it goes on, but this type of shit is campier than when Harry pulled a random sword from a hat and stabbed the basilisk. The score is much improved from the last two entries, the CGI hasn't held up the best but holds up better than rushed blockbusters do two years after release, the performances are fantastic, the animated Tale of the Three Brothers was awesome, and again... there's actual color. It was refreshing, and slightly more enjoyable than the last three entries, but still doesn't reach the heights of franchise's beginnings.

Rowling's final book, the 2010 fantasy film "Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows: Part 1" takes a decidedly darker and more contemplative turn away from the familiar halls of Hogwarts. With the Ministry of Magic falling under Lord Voldemort's control and Death Eaters tightening their grip on the wizarding world, Harry Potter, Ron Weasley, and Hermione Granger are forced into hiding as fugitives. The trio embarks on an isolated and perilous quest across the British wilderness to locate and destroy the remaining Horcruxes that hold the key to Voldemort's immortality. This movies best feature is human Ron was written and how the stress of Voldemort returning has taken its affect on not only the main cast but also the whole world. It felt very justified for how Ron acted in this situation and his frustration with the events just felt very authentic, primarily due to how he was always listening to radio to make sure his family was safe which was a trait that both Harry and Hermione had. Donny’s death was sad and didn’t feel out of place or random as they previously explained the effects of the evaporation magic. The story of the deathly hallows and three brothers were phenomenal, I loved the animated style and the way it was told was very entertaining while also having real world implications. The scene where Harry saw his parents tombstone was very emotional however it’s a shame they glanced past it very fast.the consistency with the magic has also been great from the first film to now especially the consistency with items like the invisibility cloak as it seems like something that would be ignored when it’s so useful and makes scene feel unnecessary and stupid, it’s good to see how each scene has an explanation you can infer from why they’re not using items like these. I don’t like how slow paced some scenes are especially for how long they spend in the forest hiding. I still find the humour to be funny and great as it primarily lies in scenes that aren’t tense or in scenes where a character is trying to take away from how tense it feels. The start is also awesome the clash of magic between Harry and Voldemort was cool to see and by immediately killing off the professor and injuring Ron’s brother it immediately makes it serious and displays the threat of the movie. I don’t like the evaporation magic as it seems like an instant escape button from any situation. Overall, it’s really entertaining and nerve-wrecking, however it just doesn’t do anything besides Ron’s character to an amazing degree. These movies are also beginning to stem away from their roots of having a really unique aura and vibe to it and its humour to just becoming very overly gritty because of Voldemort which I think takes away from aspects of most of these movies.
